Its highborn call themselves the sons of the harpy, after the city's emblem, a variation on the Old Ghis harpy — a woman's torso, bat wings, an eagle's legs, and a scorpion's tail, its talons clutching a whip and a slave collar. Yunkai mints its own coinage, golden marks stamped with a stepped pyramid on one face and the harpy on the other.
city-meereen: The largest of the Ghiscari Slaver Cities on Slaver's Bay, its noble families housed in stepped pyramids of colored brick rising around the eight-hundred-foot Great Pyramid at the city's heart, its thirty-three tiers echoing the sacred number of the old gods of Ghis and crowned by a towering bronze harpy, the emblem of the Slaver Cities. Ruled for thousands of years not by any king but by the slaving Great Masters, heads of the city's oldest families, Meereen has never known a monarchy. The city is ringed by massive brick walls and, like Astapor and Yunkai, traces its harpy emblem and pyramid-building tradition back to the Old Empire of Ghis, of which it was once a colony. Meereen is equally famed for its fighting pits, arenas where slaves trained as gladiators fight to the death in combats the Ghiscari regard as a sacred blood sacrifice to their gods rather than mere butchery. The grandest of these, the Great Arena of Daznak, seats some thirty thousand spectators around a vast brick bowl entered through the Gates of Fate, twin bronze statues of struggling warriors. The pits have long drawn traders and spectators from across the known world, filling Meereen's coffers and fueling its slave trade for as long as the city has stood.
city-vaes-dothrak: The City of Riders, the only permanent settlement of the nomadic Dothraki and the sacred heart of their culture, sprawling beneath the Mother of Mountains at the northeastern edge of the Dothraki Sea. Vast in area — large enough to shelter every khalasar at once — it is sparsely peopled, ruled and inhabited chiefly by slaves and the dosh khaleen, the order of widowed khaleesis whose wisdom and authority even the mightiest khal is bound to respect. Within its bounds, drawing a blade or shedding the blood of a free man is forbidden to all, making it the one place where rival khalasars can meet in safety. The Godsway, a broad avenue running from the bronze Horse Gate to the foot of the Mother of Mountains, is lined on both sides with statues, idols, and holy relics plundered from a hundred conquered peoples, a standing record of centuries of Dothraki conquest; along it lie the Western Market, where traders from the Free Cities sell their wares, and the Eastern Market, visited by merchants from Yi Ti, Asshai, the Shadow Lands, and the lands beside the Jade Sea. Outsiders are tolerated so long as they keep the city's peace and honor the dosh khaleen with the customary gifts of salt, silver, and seed. The Godsway also passes the Womb of the World, a lake the Dothraki hold sacred and believe bottomless, said to be the place from which the first man rode forth on the first horse.
ruin-old-ghis: The ruined heart of the ancient Old Empire of Ghis, one of the oldest civilizations known to history, whose lockstep legions conquered and held sway over much of Essos for thousands of years before Valyria ever rose to power. Its builders raised the great brick pyramids and towers that later Ghiscari cities would imitate, and adopted the harpy — a winged, taloned woman clutching a thunderbolt — as the empire's emblem, still borne today by Astapor, Yunkai, and Meereen as proud self-styled "sons of the harpy." Ghis fought Valyria five times over the centuries as the young Freehold's power grew, each war ending in defeat for the Ghiscari legions, since courage and discipline were no match for dragons. In the Fifth Ghiscari War, five thousand years before Aegon's Conquest, Valyrian dragons finally broke the last Ghiscari armies and burned Old Ghis itself to cinders, and the Valyrians sowed its fields with salt and sulfur to ensure the city could never rise again. With the Empire's fall, Ghiscari culture, religion, and tongue were largely lost; the Ghiscari of the Slaver Cities today speak a corrupted form of High Valyrian flavored with a scattering of old Ghiscari words, though they still write in the ancient glyphs of their ancestors.
city-new-ghis: The youngest, smallest, and most dynamic of the Ghiscari cities, an island city in the Gulf of Grief that claims to be Old Ghis reborn. Its iron legions, free men serving fixed terms rather than slaves, are trained and armed in the fashion of Astapor's Unsullied.
ruin-zamettar: A ruined city on the northern coast of Sothoryos, raised by the Ghiscari during the Old Empire before falling to Valyrian dragonlords during the Fourth Ghiscari War. Long abandoned, it was briefly resettled by Rhoynar fleeing Essos with Princess Nymeria, but disease and unexplained disappearances soon emptied it again.
ruin-yeen: A ruined city on the Zamoyos in Sothoryos, built entirely of massive blocks of oily black stone whose origin remains one of the great mysteries of the known world. Rhoynar fleeing with Princess Nymeria briefly settled there amid constant attacks from jungle ghouls, before its people vanished without explanation.
ruin-gogossos: Gogossos, once called Gorgai, is a ruined city on the Isle of Tears, founded by the Old Empire of Ghis before being captured and renamed by Valyrian dragonlords, who used it as a penal colony notorious for torture and blood magic. During the Century of Blood it grew wealthy on slavery and sorcery as the so-called Tenth Free City, until the Red Death plague emerged from its slave pens and left it abandoned.
castle-flints-finger: The seat of House Flint of Flint's Finger, a minor branch of the Flint family in the southwestern North. Once held by the Ironborn, it now swears fealty to House Bolton as Wardens of the North.
city-barrowton: A town in the North built around the Great Barrow, a great hill topped by Barrow Hall, the seat of House Dustin. Reputed to hold the grave of the First King of the First Men, the barrow gives the barrowlands their name, and the Dustins have ruled as bannermen of House Stark since the last Barrow King submitted at the end of the Thousand Years War.
castle-torrhens-square: The seat of House Tallhart, a stone-walled castle south of the wolfswood and north of Barrowton. Its lords are among the principal houses sworn to House Stark, bearing three green sentinel trees on a brown field.
ruin-bhorash: A ruined city on the northern coast of Slaver's Bay, south of the Painted Mountains, linked by old Valyrian roads to Mantarys and Tolos.
castle-pyke: The seat of House Greyjoy, Lord Reaper of Pyke, and ruling castle of the Iron Islands, standing on the island of Pyke off the western coast of Westeros. It was originally raised as a single stronghold atop a rocky headland, but centuries of erosion by the sea have crumbled the cliff beneath it, leaving several of its keeps and towers stranded on separate wave-battered stone stacks connected only by narrow bridges of rope, plank, and carved stone. The oldest and outermost of these, the Sea Tower, rises from its own crooked pillar of rock and can only be reached by crossing three such bridges, the last of hempen rope. Within the Great Keep, the castle's central hall, stands the Seastone Chair, the ancient seat of the Lords Reaper. After Aegon the Conqueror's dragonfire ended House Hoare's rule over the Iron Islands, a kingsmoot elected Vickon Greyjoy, already Lord of Pyke, as the new ruler of the isles, and the castle has remained House Greyjoy's seat ever since. Centuries later, its walls were breached and its old south tower destroyed when King Robert Baratheon stormed Pyke to crush Balon Greyjoy's rebellion against the Iron Throne.
other-pebbleton: A fishing village on the eastern coast of Great Wyk in the Iron Islands, seat of House Merlyn. A square towerhouse with corner turrets overlooks the surrounding hovels, home to several thousand people who work the local fisheries.
castle-hammerhorn: The seat of the main line of House Goodbrother, a large square castle with spiked iron battlements set in the Hardstone Hills of southwestern Great Wyk. Unlike most Ironborn strongholds, its wealth comes not from the sea but from the mines beneath it.
ruin-naggas-ribs: Forty-four towering stone ribs on Nagga's Hill on Old Wyk, believed to be the remains of a sea dragon slain in the Age of Heroes. Legend holds that the Grey King raised his hall from Nagga's bones, and the site remains sacred ground where the Ironborn hold their kingsmoots to choose a king.
castle-ten-towers: The seat of House Harlaw on the isle of Harlaw, the richest and most populous of the Iron Islands. Built by the mercurial Lord Theomore Harlaw after he blamed the damp of the old Harlaw Hall for the deaths of his infant sons, it consists of ten dissimilar towers joined by wallwalks and covered bridges.
castle-faircastle: The seat of House Farman on Fair Isle off the Westerlands coast, an ancient First Men line that once ruled the island as petty kings and guarded the western coast from Ironborn raiders. The Farmans knelt to House Lannister generations before the Conquest, sealing the union through marriage to the last Farman king's daughter.
ruin-tyria: A ruined city across the Smoking Sea from the isle of Oros, founded as a Valyrian colony ruled by governors from the Freehold rather than by self-rule. Connected to the city of Valyria by an ancient road before the Doom, its ruins remain inhabited to some degree even now.
ruin-valyria: The capital of the Valyrian Freehold, the greatest civilization Essos had ever known, its dragonlords ruling much of the continent for five thousand years from a city built across the Fourteen Fires, a chain of volcanoes the Valyrians believed to be the ancestral home of dragons. Valyria rose in terraces up the mountainsides, its fountains, towers, and manses housing the forty dragonlord families who bred and rode dragons drawn to the volcanoes' heat, while their slaves mined the surrounding peaks for metal and lesser mysteries. In 102 BC, roughly a century before Aegon's Conquest, the Doom of Valyria struck without warning: every hill for five hundred miles erupted at once, filling the sky with ash and fire hot enough to kill dragons in their lairs, while earthquakes toppled palaces and boiling lakes turned to acid. The catastrophe shattered the Valyrian peninsula into fragments and drowned it beneath the volcanic Smoking Sea, ending the Freehold's five-thousand-year reign in a single day. Valyria itself was left an ash-choked ruin half-swallowed by the sea, its smoking bones said to be overrun with demons, and sailors hold that any who so much as glimpse its fiery mountains rising from the waves will soon meet a dreadful death. To this day no ship dares approach it, and Valyria endures as one of the most feared and cursed places in the known world.
city-qarth: The Queen of Cities, an ancient port on Essos's southern coast controlling the Jade Gates between the Summer and Jade Seas, one of the great crossroads of trade in the known world. Its triple walls — ranked among the wonders of the world by the travel-writer Lomas Longstrider — rise in tiers around the city: an outer wall of red sandstone carved with animals, a middle wall of grey granite carved with scenes of war, and an innermost wall of black marble carved with scenes of lovemaking, their gates banded in copper, iron, and gold. These walls spared Qarth the fate of other Qaathi cities destroyed by the Dothraki during the Century of Blood. The city is contested by three rival powers: the Pureborn, ceremonial descendants of Qarth's ancient kings who sit the Hall of a Thousand Thrones but hold little true power; the Thirteen, merchant princes who between them own perhaps a thousand ships and command the city's trade and wealth; and the warlocks of the House of the Undying, a once-mighty order now much diminished, who dwell in a windowless grey ruin coiled like a stone serpent amid a grove of black-barked trees and are said to drink shade of the evening, brewed from those trees' leaves, to sustain their fading powers.
city-lord-hewetts-town: A large port town on the island of Oakenshield in the Reach, seat of House Hewett and twice the size of Lordsport on Pyke. It is one of the chief settlements of the Shield Islands, which guard the mouth of the Mander against raiders from the Iron Islands.
castle-casterly-rock: The seat of House Lannister and Warden of the West, carved into a colossal stone hill overlooking Lannisport and the Sunset Sea. Rather than a conventional walled castle, Casterly Rock is a promontory hollowed out from within: centuries of mining opened up a warren of halls, galleries, stairways, and chambers inside the stone itself, honeycombed further by the gold and silver mines that are the source of House Lannister's wealth. Its main gate, the Lion's Mouth, is a vast natural cavern on the Rock's landward face, reached by a stone stair broad enough for twenty riders abreast; sea gates on its western face open onto hidden caverns sheltering the Lannisters' own docks and shipyards. Seen from a distance, the Rock's silhouette is said to resemble a crouching lion. According to legend, it was won in the Age of Heroes by Lann the Clever, who tricked the First Men house of Casterly into abandoning it — in some versions by filling it with vermin, in others by smuggling in lions to kill its lords. Lann's descendants ruled the westerlands from the Rock for thousands of years as Kings of the Rock, a title lost only when Aegon the Conqueror's invasion reduced House Lannister to Lords of Casterly Rock and Wardens of the West.
ruin-hardhome: An abandoned free folk settlement beyond the Wall, built beneath a great cliff riddled with caves on a sheltered natural harbor at the tip of Storrold's Point. It was once close to becoming the only true town north of the Wall, but its inhabitants perished when the settlement burned in a catastrophic, unexplained fire some six centuries past — a blaze so vast that the Night's Watch on the Wall mistook it for a false dawn. In recent years its ruins have again drawn free folk fleeing south ahead of the encroaching cold beyond the Wall.
castle-mormont-keep: The seat of House Mormont on Bear Island, a modest wood-walled castle with a smoky great hall built of huge logs, ringed by an earthen palisade rather than stone walls. Its gate bears a carving of a woman in a bearskin, a suckling child on one arm and a battleaxe in the other, reflecting the island's remote and impoverished character compared to grander seats of the North.
castle-driftmark: The ancestral seat of House Velaryon in the Crownlands, standing on the southern shore of the island of Driftmark in Blackwater Bay, with the port town of Hull spread beneath its walls. A damp, often-flooded castle, it was settled before House Targaryen's arrival at nearby Dragonstone, when Velaryon ships gave the family control of the middle of the Narrow Sea. Its cramped, waterlogged halls later led Lord Corlys Velaryon, the Sea Snake, to build a new seat, High Tide, elsewhere on the island.
city-lotus-point: A modest port town in southwestern Walano, the northernmost and most populous of the Summer Isles' three major islands, lying north of the smaller island of Koj. It shares Walano's southern coast with the settlement of Tall Trees Town, while the town of Last Lament lies on the island's northern shore. Little else about the town is recorded, and maps in The Lands of Ice and Fire mislabel it as 'Lotus Port.'
city-last-lament: A town on the northern coast of Walano, the northernmost of the major Summer Islands, lying south of the island of Stone Head.
city-hesh: One of the three main settlements of Lhazar, lying northwest of Lhazosh and west of Kosrak in the semi-arid grasslands south of the Dothraki Sea. A trade route runs from Hesh through the Khyzai Pass to Meereen.
city-kosrak: One of the three main settlements of Lhazar, standing on a tributary of the Skahazadhan river east of Hesh and northeast of Lhazosh. A trade route runs southeast from Kosrak across the Red Waste to the ruined city of Vaes Tolorro.
city-lhazosh: One of the three main settlements of Lhazar, lying southeast of Hesh and southwest of Kosrak in the grasslands south of the Dothraki Sea. Trade routes run southeast from Lhazosh across the Red Waste to the ruined cities of Vaes Orvik and Vaes Shirosi.
city-ebonhead: A settlement at the mouth of the Sweet Lotus Vale on the western side of the island of Jhala in the Summer Isles, with the island of Xon and Parrot Bay lying to the east. Jhala is the southernmost and largest of the three major Summer Islands.
other-ruby-ford: A crossing of the Trident in the eastern Riverlands, named for the rubies scattered from Prince Rhaegar Targaryen's armor during the fighting there. The Battle of the Trident, fought at this ford between Robert Baratheon and Rhaegar Targaryen, was the decisive engagement of Robert's Rebellion, deciding the war in the rebels' favor. Its fords saw further clashes years later during the War of the Five Kings, when Lannister forces attacked the rearguard of a northern army crossing the river.
city-saath: A small, white-walled port city at the western end of the Sarne river delta on the Shivering Sea coast, in northern Essos. Its people, who still call themselves the Tagaez Fen, or Tall Men, are the last remnant of the once-mighty Kingdom of Sarnor, whose other cities were destroyed by the Dothraki during the Century of Blood. Saath survives largely through trade with Ib and Lorath, including the nearby Lorathi colony of Morosh, though its population has dwindled from the millions Sarnor once had to fewer than twenty thousand.
city-morosh: A fishing and mining colony of Lorath on the Shivering Sea coast, at the northern end of the Sarne river delta in northern Essos. It lies northeast of its trading partner Saath and northwest of the ruined city of Vaes Graddakh.
ruin-vaes-graddakh-sarys: A ruined city in the Sarne river delta of the Kingdom of Sarnor, west of Saath and southwest of Morosh. Formerly called Sarys, it was the last Sarnori city to fall to the Dothraki, taken by the khalasar of Khal Zeggo near the end of the Century of Blood after its people had already fled; the Dothraki renamed the ruins Vaes Graddakh, meaning City of Filth.
ruin-vaes-khadokh-essaria: A ruined city east of the Forest of Qohor, on the western border of the Kingdom of Sarnor. Formerly called Essaria and remembered as the Lost Free City, it was a Valyrian Freehold colony that prospered from trade with the Sarnori to the east until the Dothraki destroyed it and slaughtered its people during the Century of Blood. The Dothraki renamed the ruins Vaes Khadokh, meaning City of Corpses.
ruin-vaes-khewo-sarnath: The ruined seat of the High Kings of Sarnor, on the Sarne River in the southern Kingdom of Sarnor. Formerly called Sarnath of the Tall Towers, it was the greatest of the Sarnori cities and held the fabled Palace With a Thousand Rooms. After the last high king, Mazor Alexi, gathered an army beneath its walls that was destroyed at the Field of Crows during the Century of Blood, Khal Loso the Lame captured and burned the city two weeks later. The Dothraki renamed the ruins Vaes Khewo, meaning City of Worms.
ruin-vojjor-samui-kasath: A ruined city on the Sarne River in the Kingdom of Sarnor, known to the Sarnori as the City of Caravans. After the Dothraki devastated Sathar during the Century of Blood, Kasath and Gornath both sent armies to plunder its remains, only to clash with each other over the spoils; six years later, Khal Moro, allied to Gornath by marriage, conquered Kasath itself. The Dothraki renamed the ruins Vojjor Samvi, meaning the Broken Gods.
ruin-yalli-qamayi-sathar: A ruined city in the southeastern Kingdom of Sarnor, on the edge of the Dothraki Sea. Formerly called Sathar, the Waterfall City, and said to have been the loveliest of the Sarnori grassland cities, it was the first Sarnori city burned by the Dothraki during the Century of Blood; its men were put to the sword and its women and children enslaved, most dying during the march to Hazdahn Mo. Khal Moro himself named the ruins Yalli Qamayi, meaning the Wailing Children.
ruin-vaes-leqse-gornath: A ruined city beside one of the lakes remaining from the ancient Silver Sea, in the eastern Kingdom of Sarnor. Formerly called Gornath by the Lake, its king allied himself with Khal Moro after the Dothraki sacked Sathar, even taking one of the khal's daughters as a wife. Twelve years later, when Khal Horro overthrew Moro and besieged the city in turn, the king was killed by his own Dothraki wife, who married Horro afterward. The Dothraki renamed the ruins Vaes Leqse, meaning City of Rats.
ruin-vaes-athjikhari-sallosh: A ruined city on the Silver Shore in the eastern Kingdom of Sarnor, once known as Sallosh. Called the City of Scholars, it held a great library recording the history of the Tall Men, until the Dothraki burned the city and its library alike during the Century of Blood. The Dothraki renamed the ruins Vaes Athjikhari, meaning City of Sickness.
ruin-vaes-diaf-hazdahn-mo: A ruined Ghiscari hill city in the Dothraki Sea, south of the Kingdom of Sarnor and north of Meereen. Formerly the Ghiscari slave market of Hazdahn Mo (rendered Hazdahn No on some maps), it was where the enslaved women and children of Sathar were marched after that city's fall during the Century of Blood, though three-quarters of them died along the way; the city itself was later destroyed by the Dothraki in the same century. The Dothraki renamed the ruins Vaes Diaf, meaning City of the Skull.
ruin-krazaaj-has-ghardaq: A ruined Ghiscari city between the southeastern Dothraki Sea and Lhazar, on a tributary of the eastern Skahazadhan, west of Vaes Mejhah and east of Meereen. Formerly called Ghardaq, it was one of the northern Ghiscari colonies destroyed by the Dothraki during the Century of Blood that followed the Doom of Valyria. The Dothraki renamed the ruins Krazaaj Has, meaning Sharp Mountains, after its Ghiscari pyramids.
ruin-vaes-mejhah: A ruined Ghiscari city between the southeastern Dothraki Sea and Lhazar, on a tributary of the eastern Skahazadhan, between Vaes Efe and Krazaaj Has. It was destroyed, like other Ghiscari colonies of the region, by the Dothraki after the Doom of Valyria; its Dothraki name means City of Whores.
ruin-vaes-efe: A ruined Ghiscari city in the southeastern Dothraki Sea, south of Vaes Dothrak and north of the Skahazadhan, with Vaes Mejhah and Krazaaj Has to the southwest. One of several Ghiscari settlements destroyed by the Dothraki during the Century of Blood, its name in the Dothraki language means City of Shackles.
ruin-vaes-jini-yinishar: A ruined city on the Stone Road in the foothills of the western Bone Mountains, southwest of Adakhakileki. Formerly called Yinishar, it was renamed Vaes Jini by the Dothraki, meaning City of Goats.
ruin-adakhakileki: A ruined city on the northern edge of the red waste, near the Poison Sea and the Stone Road, in the foothills of the western Bone Mountains. Its original name has been lost, and it is known only by its Dothraki name, Adakhakileki, meaning the Cannibals, suggesting that it too fell to the Dothraki.
ruin-vaes-tolorro: An abandoned city in the red waste beyond the Dothraki Sea, likely one of four cities of the region once inhabited by the Qaathi before the Dothraki sacked them. Surrounded by cracked white walls with broken gates and a maze of narrow, windowless streets, it was given its current Dothraki name, meaning City of Bones, by Daenerys Targaryen, who sheltered there with her khalasar while crossing the waste.
ruin-vaes-qosar: A ruined Qaathi city in the southeastern red waste, east of Qarkash and northwest of Qarth. It was destroyed by the Dothraki during the Century of Blood, who renamed it Vaes Qosar, meaning City of Spiders. Daenerys Targaryen and her khalasar passed its ruins while traveling from Vaes Tolorro to Qarth.
ruin-vaes-shirosi: A ruined Qaathi town in the southwestern red waste, north of Qarkash and Port Yhos. It was destroyed by the Dothraki during the Century of Blood, who renamed it Vaes Shirosi, meaning City of Scorpions.
ruin-vaes-orvik: A ruined Qaathi city in the southwestern red waste, north of Port Yhos. It was destroyed by the Dothraki during the Century of Blood, who renamed it Vaes Orvik, or City of the Whip, after the great number of slaves taken when it fell.
city-qarkash: A Qartheen town on the shores of the Summer Sea, east of Slaver's Bay and south of the red waste. It lies west of Qarth, with Port Yhos situated further along the coast to the west.
city-port-yhos: A town on the shores of the Summer Sea, southeast of Slaver's Bay. As the westernmost settlement under Qarth's control, it lies south of Vaes Orvik and southwest of the red waste.
ruin-gorosh: A ruined city on the northern coast of Wyvern Point in Sothoryos, once a grim penal colony founded by the Old Empire of Ghis. Little else is known of it, as the jungles of Sothoryos remain largely unexplored.
city-faros: A city at the mouth of a river on the northern coast of Great Moraq, the largest island in the known world. Its inhabitants worship a deity known as the Stone Cow, and Qartheen say it is easier to milk the Stone Cow of Faros than to wring gold from the Pureborn.
city-vahar: A city on the island of the same name, in the Cinnamon Straits between Great Moraq to the east and Lesser Moraq to the west. The island has grown wealthy from the spice trade.
city-port-moraq: A port city on the southern coast of Great Moraq, near the Cinnamon Straits, with dense rainforest to its north and the Isle of Elephants to its south. It is a regular stop for traders returning from the Jade Sea.
city-zabhad: The chief port on the northern shore of the Isle of Elephants in the Jade Sea, and the only known settlement on the island. It is visited by traders following the Jade Sea's southern trading circle, alongside Port Moraq.
ruin-vaes-leisi: An abandoned settlement of carved trees and haunted grottoes on a small peninsula in the western Kingdom of the Ifequevron, jutting into the Shivering Sea. It was the last known dwelling of the Ifequevron, a small, shy forest people believed by many maesters to be kin to the children of the forest, who vanished from the region, possibly wiped out by the Ibbenese or driven into hiding. The Dothraki, whose name for the Ifequevron means those who walk among the trees, renamed the ruins Vaes Leisi, or City of Ghosts.
ruin-vaes-aresak-ibbish: A ruined Ibbenese colony on the Shivering Sea coast of northern Essos, in the forest that was once home to the Kingdom of the Ifequevron. Formerly called Ibbish, it grew from a fishing village into a fortified port with a deep, walled harbor, until Dothraki khalasars began raiding it during the Century of Blood, sacking it repeatedly and forcing thousands of its women into slavery. The Dothraki renamed the ruins Vaes Aresak, meaning City of Cowards, after its people retreated to Ib rather than face an approaching khalasar.
city-new-ibbish: An Ibbenese town on a forested peninsula of mainland Essos, north of the Kingdom of the Ifequevron, with the Bay of Whales to its north. It was founded after the Dothraki destroyed the older Ibbenese mainland settlements roughly two centuries ago, leaving the ruins of Ibbish—now called Vaes Aresak by the Dothraki—to the southeast.
city-ib-sar: The only Ibbenese town on Far Ib, the second-largest of the Ibbenese isles, a bleaker and poorer land than Ib itself, though similarly forested and mountainous. It was originally founded as a place of exile, where the Ibbenese of old sent their most notorious criminals, often after mutilating them so they could never return home.
city-ib-nor: One of the two principal towns on Ib, the largest island of Ibben, situated on its stony, mountainous north coast amid ancient forests and rushing rivers. Ibben itself is an island nation in the Shivering Sea, north of Essos.
city-port-of-ibben: The largest and richest city of the Shivering Sea, on the southern coast of the island of Ib and the capital of Ibben. Grey and gloomy, it is built of cobbled alleys climbing steep hills, its busy docks and shipyards lit through the long nights by whale-oil lamps hung on iron chains. Its wealth comes chiefly from the bone, blubber, and oil brought back by Ibbenese whalers, who range the Shivering Sea and the icy waters beyond in search of their catch. The ruins of the castle of the Kings-Gods loom over the port, a relic of the God-Kings who once ruled Ibben as living deities until their line ended with the Doom of Valyria; power today rests with an elected Shadow Council, chosen by the Thousand, an assembly of wealthy guildsmen, ancient nobles, and priests and priestesses not unlike the magisters of the Free Cities. The Ibbenese themselves are a short, broad-shouldered, and heavily built people, seldom standing more than five and a half feet tall, and are said to be the hairiest folk in the known world. Foreign visitors to the port are confined to its harbor precincts and may venture further only in the rare company of an Ibbenese host. Roughly two centuries ago, Dothraki khalasars began raiding Ibbenese holdings on the Essos mainland at Far Ib, and in one of the more celebrated clashes the Ibbenese broke the khalasar of Khal Onqo.
city-kayakayanaya: One of three fortress cities of the former Patrimony of Hyrkoon, standing on the Steel Road in the Bone Mountains east of the Great Sand Sea. Its walls of black basalt, black iron, and yellow bone were raised to guard the realm's western marches, and for centuries the city has weathered attacks from the Jogos Nhai. Like its sister cities Bayasabhad and Samyriana, it is ruled by the Great Fathers, whose daughters are trained as warriors from childhood while sons are gelded on reaching manhood.
city-samyriana: One of three fortress cities of the former Patrimony of Hyrkoon, carved of grey stone into the eastern Bone Mountains where the Stone Road passes near the Great Sand Sea. Like its sister cities Kayakayanaya and Bayasabhad, it was raised to guard the realm's western marches from outlaws and the wild men of the mountains, and it is ruled today by the Great Fathers, whose daughters are trained as warriors from childhood while sons are gelded on reaching manhood.
city-bayasabhad: One of three fortress cities of the former Patrimony of Hyrkoon, known as the City of Snakes, guarding the eastern end of the Sand Road through the southern Bone Mountains. Like its sister cities Kayakayanaya and Samyriana, it was raised to guard the realm's western marches, and it is ruled today by the Great Fathers, whose daughters are trained as warriors from childhood while sons are gelded on reaching manhood.
city-tiqui: A city in the western hills of Yi Ti, southeast of the Great Sand Sea and linked by the Sand Road to Qarth and Bayasabhad. It served as the capital of the Golden Empire under the Purple Emperors and remains an important market city today.
city-trader-town: A crude, sprawling garrison city in Yi Ti, seat of a general who has proclaimed himself God-Emperor in defiance of the ruling azure emperor at Yin. Unlike the empire's ancient capitals, it grew up around military encampments rather than royal design.
city-asabhad: A city on the western border of Yi Ti near the Bone Mountains and the Jade Gates, linked by trade road to Qarth and Yin. It is a minor waypoint known mostly from maps, with little else recorded about it.
city-yin: The great port city of Yi Ti on the Jade Sea, seat of the Golden Empire and capital under most of its ruling dynasties, each known by a color: the Grey, Indigo, and Pearl-White Emperors ruled from Yin in earlier ages, and the reigning Azure Emperors — now in their seventeenth generation — hold court there again today. Yi Ti's priestly scribes trace Yin's lineage back to the legendary Great Empire of the Dawn, said to have stretched from the Shivering Sea to the Jade Sea under its first ruler, the God-on-Earth, son of the Lion of Night and the Maiden-Made-of-Light, who reigned for ten thousand years before ascending to the stars. The city's imperial palace is said to be larger than all of King's Landing, vast enough to house the entire court and household of a god-emperor. Over the long history of the Golden Empire, its capital has shifted away from Yin more than once, to cities such as Tiqui and Jinqi, before returning each time. Though ancient tradition still styles its god-emperors absolute rulers, real power today rests increasingly with local governors and tax farmers, who have carved the provinces into a hundred lesser princedoms.
city-jinqi: A city on the coast of the Jade Sea in Yi Ti, near a river delta north of the island of Leng. It served as the martial capital of the Maroon Emperors, who kept court there to better guard the empire's frontier against raiders from the Shadow Lands.
city-asshai: A vast port city at the mouth of the Ash River on the Jade Sea, at the southernmost tip of the Shadow Lands, often called Asshai-by-the-Shadow. Its walls, streets, and buildings are built entirely of a black stone greasy to the touch that seems to drink the light, and its walls alone are said to be large enough to enclose Volantis, Qarth, King's Landing, and Oldtown combined — yet the city holds no more people than a good-sized market town, and by night only one building in ten shows a light. No children are seen in its streets, and its masked or veiled inhabitants seldom go about on foot, preferring palanquins of ebony and iron carried by slaves behind drawn curtains. Asshai welcomes practitioners of every dark art — warlocks, red priests, bloodmages, and shadowbinders — and is said to forbid nothing. Its ancient books are the source of the prophecy of Azor Ahai, the promised champion of R'hllor said to be reborn amid smoke and salt, and the city is widely held to be the origin point of the Lord of Light's faith. Even Asshai's own shadowbinders fear to travel far up the Ash River, where the ruined corpse city of Stygai broods in the mountains beyond, and few travelers to Asshai itself are ever seen to return.
ruin-stygai: A ruined city in the heart of the Shadow Lands, known as the City of Night for the brief hour each day when sunlight reaches its streets. Demons and dragons are said to lurk among its ruins, and even the shadowbinders of Asshai fear to approach it.
city-leng-yi: A town on the northern shore of the island of Leng, more akin in appearance to the Yi Ti cities of Yin and Jinqi than to Turrani in the island's south.
city-leng-ma: A town on the western shore of the island of Leng, near a river mouth, likewise more reminiscent of the Yi Ti cities of Yin and Jinqi than of Turrani to the south.
city-turrani: A town on the southern shore of the island of Leng, near a river mouth and north of the Manticore Isles. Unlike the Yi Ti-descended towns of Leng Yi and Leng Ma in the north, Turrani is home to the native Lengii culture.
city-carcosa: A legendary city on the southeastern shore of the Hidden Sea, within the Mountains of the Morn in far eastern Essos. It is the seat in exile of a sorcerer lord who claims to be the sixty-ninth Yellow Emperor of Yi Ti, a dynasty that fell thousands of years ago.
city-city-of-the-winged-men: A legendary city on the northwestern shore of the Hidden Sea, within the Mountains of the Morn in far eastern Essos, facing Carcosa across the water. Little else is known of it beyond its name and location.
city-bonetown: A rumored town in the Grey Waste of far eastern Essos, said to be built entirely of bone and named for the strange, ancient bones traded there from the nearby Dry Deep.
city-k-dath: A city in the Grey Waste of far eastern Essos, said to be the site of unspeakable rites performed to satisfy the hunger of mad gods — so feared that even the Shrykes to its south dare not approach. Its people claim it to be the oldest city in the known world.
city-nefer: Called the Secret City by travelers, the capital and last remaining city of the kingdom of N'Ghai, a port at a river mouth on the Shivering Sea in far eastern Essos. Shrouded in fog and hemmed by chalk cliffs, nine-tenths of it lies underground, and centuries of raids by the Jogos Nhai have reduced N'Ghai to this single city.
castle-harvest-hall: The seat of House Selmy, marcher lords of the Dornish Marches in the Stormlands, near the eastern border of the Reach. The house is known for its archers, and its most celebrated son, Ser Barristan Selmy, earned the epithet "the Bold" before rising to the Kingsguard.
ruin-vaes-gorqoyi-mardosh: A ruined city on the Sarne River in the Kingdom of Sarnor, once called Mardosh the Impregnable or the City of Soldiers for its heavy fortifications. Cut off and besieged for nearly six years during the Century of Blood, its defenders were finally driven by starvation to kill their own wives and children rather than see them enslaved, then threw open the gates for one last, suicidal charge in which every last man died. The Dothraki renamed the ruins Vaes Gorqoyi, meaning the City of the Bloody Charge.
other-field-of-crows: The site in the grasslands of the Kingdom of Sarnor, between Sarnath and the ruins of Kasath, where four Dothraki khalasars numbering eighty thousand riders crushed the last army of the united Sarnori kingdoms during the Century of Blood, ending organized resistance to the Dothraki conquest of Sarnor.
ruin-sarhoy: A ruined port city of the Rhoynar, once a great rival to Volantis, built at one of the four mouths of the Rhoyne on the Summer Sea. During the Second Spice War, Volantis and three Valyrian dragonlords destroyed Sarhoy with dragonfire and sowed its ruins with salt to keep it from ever rising again, enslaving those who survived. Princess Nymeria's fleet passed its ruins on its way down the Rhoyne before she led the Rhoynar on to Dorne. Sarhoy remains a desolate, reputedly haunted ruin to this day.
the-new-gift: A strip of land stretching twenty-five leagues south from the Wall, granted to the Night's Watch by King Jaehaerys I at the urging of his sister-wife, Queen Alysanne, after she was moved by the Watch's dedication during a visit to the Wall on her dragon Silverwing. The grant doubled the Watch's territory, adding to the older Brandon's Gift immediately to its north and giving the order fifty leagues of land in total to draw upon. Lord Alaric Stark of Winterfell resented ceding the territory, fearing the Watch would neglect it in favor of matters beyond the Wall. Though it remains under the Night's Watch's authority, the New Gift has grown increasingly empty over the centuries as the order's ranks have thinned, with much of its land left untended.
riverlands: Home to House Tully, Lords Paramount of the Trident, ruling from the castle of Riverrun where the Tumblestone meets the Red Fork. Watered by the three forks of the Trident and open on every side, the region has no natural frontiers and was for centuries divided among rival First Men river kings, most notably the Mudds, who united much of the riverlands as Kings of the Rivers and the Hills, and the long-feuding Houses Blackwood and Bracken. During the Andal invasion the river lords briefly set aside their quarrels to resist the newcomers, but were defeated, and the land later fell under the rule of the Ironborn Kings of the Isles and the Rivers. The last of these, Harren the Black of House Hoare, raised the vast castle of Harrenhal using the forced labor of the river lords he had subjugated. When Aegon the Conqueror marched on Harrenhal, the river lords rose against Harren under Lord Edmyn Tully of Riverrun, the first Riverlands lord to join Aegon's cause; after Harren and his line died in the castle's burning, Aegon named Tully Lord Paramount of the Trident, a title House Tully has held ever since. Its exposed, borderless position has made the Riverlands one of the most fought-over regions of Westeros in the centuries that followed.
beyond-the-wall: The vast, unclaimed territory north of the Wall, lying beyond the authority of the Seven Kingdoms and the Iron Throne. It stretches from the haunted forest through the icy peaks of the Frostfangs to the desolate Lands of Always Winter in the far north. Its scattered inhabitants, known to southerners as wildlings but calling themselves the free folk, answer to no crown, following their own chieftains and, on rare occasions, uniting behind a self-proclaimed King-Beyond-the-Wall. According to legend, the first such king, Joramun, allied with Brandon the Breaker, King of Winter, to overthrow the Night's King, a corrupted Lord Commander of the Night's Watch who had ruled the Nightfort for thirteen years with a mysterious queen at his side. Centuries later, in 226 AC, Raymun Redbeard led the free folk in a breach of the Wall, only to be destroyed by the Starks and Umbers at the Battle at Long Lake. The region's harsh climate and old magic have long kept the Seven Kingdoms wary of what may lie beyond the Wall.
brandons-gift: A strip of land some twenty-five leagues wide, stretching south from the Wall, granted to the Night's Watch in perpetuity for its provisioning and upkeep. Tradition holds that it was granted by Brandon the Builder, the legendary Stark king credited with raising the Wall itself, though some maesters argue it was granted by another Brandon of House Stark. For thousands of years the Watch's stewards farmed the land, but as the order's numbers dwindled, much of it reverted to wilderness. Rather than being held by any bannerman lord, it remains under the direct administration of the Night's Watch and its Lord Commander; it was later doubled in size when Queen Alysanne Targaryen persuaded her husband, King Jaehaerys I the Conciliator, to grant the neighboring New Gift.
the-north: The northernmost and largest of the Seven Kingdoms, ruled by House Stark as Wardens of the North from their seat at Winterfell. According to legend it was united by Brandon the Builder during the Age of Heroes, and the Starks ruled it afterward as Kings of Winter for thousands of years. It was the only kingdom to turn back the Andal invasion, when King Theon Stark broke the war-band of Argos Sevenstar at the Weeping Water and carried the fighting into Andalos itself. The North joined the Seven Kingdoms without a battle: on learning of Aegon the Conqueror's victories at Harrenhal and the Field of Fire, Torrhen Stark, remembered as the King Who Knelt, submitted and was made Lord of Winterfell and Warden of the North. Centuries later, the deaths of Lord Rickard Stark and his heir Brandon at the hands of King Aerys II Targaryen helped ignite Robert's Rebellion, in which the North's armies under Eddard Stark helped end Targaryen rule of the Seven Kingdoms.
the-iron-islands: An archipelago off the western coast of Westeros, currently ruled by House Greyjoy as Lords Reaper of Pyke, vassals of the Iron Throne. Its people, the Ironborn, are seafaring raiders and reavers who worship the Drowned God; before Aegon's Conquest, disputes over succession were settled by a kingsmoot of ship captains and priests, a tradition older than the Andals' arrival. According to legend, the isles were first united under the Grey King during the Age of Heroes, from whom many great houses—including the Greyjoys—claim descent. Hereditary rule later passed to House Greyiron and then House Hoare, whose last king, Harren the Black, extended his dominion over the riverlands as well before Aegon the Conqueror burned him alive in Harrenhal, ending his dynasty. In the conquest's aftermath, a kingsmoot chose House Greyjoy to rule the isles as Lords of Pyke under the new crown. Centuries later, Lord Balon Greyjoy led a failed rebellion against King Robert Baratheon in an attempt to win back the islands' independence.
dorne: The southernmost of the Seven Kingdoms, ruled by House Martell from the castle of Sunspear, whose heads carry the Rhoynish title of Prince or Princess of Dorne rather than Lord or Lady. Its culture and law differ markedly from the rest of Westeros, shaped by the Rhoynar who fled the Valyrian dragonlords under Princess Nymeria and settled in southern Dorne. Nymeria's marriage to Lord Mors Martell and the ensuing Nymeria's War united the peninsula under House Nymeros Martell, which retained Rhoynish customs such as equal inheritance rights for women. Alone among the Seven Kingdoms, Dorne successfully resisted Aegon's Conquest, as the aged Princess Meria Martell refused Rhaenys Targaryen's demand to yield Sunspear. The Dornish Wars that followed, fought intermittently across several Targaryen reigns, failed to bring Dorne under the Iron Throne by force. Dorne was finally united with the rest of the Seven Kingdoms not by conquest but by marriage, when Prince Maron Martell wed Princess Daenerys Targaryen in 187 AC, securing special privileges for Dorne — including the retention of its princely title — in exchange for fealty.
stormlands: A coastal kingdom along Westeros's storm-battered southeastern shore, held since Aegon's Conquest by House Baratheon from their seat at Storm's End. According to legend, the first Storm King, Durran Godsgrief, built the castle and won the love of Elenei, daughter of the sea and storm gods; when the gods destroyed his hall in their fury, he defied them by raising fortress after fortress until the seventh withstood their wrath — a stronghold that has never fallen to siege or storm since. His line, House Durrandon, ruled as Storm Kings for thousands of years, at its height stretching from the Dornish Marches to the Trident, though the riverlands were lost to Harwin Hoar of the Iron Islands some three centuries before the Conquest. The last Storm King, Argilac the Arrogant, was slain at the Last Storm near the Bronze Gate by Orys Baratheon, reputedly Aegon I's half-brother. Orys married Argilac's daughter Argella and took up the Durrandon coat of arms and motto to found House Baratheon. Generations later, the stormlord Robert Baratheon led the rebellion that toppled the Targaryen dynasty and won him the Iron Throne.
the-vale: A dramatic, mountain-ringed valley in the east of Westeros, reachable chiefly by a single narrow road guarded by mountain clans, and ruled by House Arryn from the castle of the Eyrie, styled Warden of the East. It was the first region of Westeros where the Andals landed, and when their petty kings warred with the First Men rulers of the valley, the Andals rallied behind Ser Artys Arryn; after Artys defeated and killed the First Man king Robar Royce at the Battle of the Seven Stars, the surviving First Men houses swore fealty to him as King of Mountain and Vale, and the region became known as the Vale of Arryn. Arryn tradition conflates Artys with the Winged Knight, an older, half-legendary hero of the Age of Heroes said to have slain the Griffin King, though the two figures are thought to have lived thousands of years apart. When Aegon the Conqueror's sister Visenya landed her dragon Vhagar in the Eyrie's own courtyard, House Arryn chose to submit peacefully rather than fight, and was allowed to keep the Vale as lords rather than kings, a position it has held as Warden of the East ever since.
the-westerlands: The westernmost of the Seven Kingdoms, a coastal region whose gold and silver mines make House Lannister of Casterly Rock the wealthiest of the great houses. According to legend, it was founded by Lann the Clever, a cunning rogue of the Age of Heroes said to have won Casterly Rock from the Casterly family through wit alone rather than conquest. His descendants ruled the westerlands for thousands of years as Kings of the Rock. During Aegon's Conquest, King Loren I Lannister, called Loren the Last, allied with Mern IX Gardener of the Reach against the invading Targaryens, but their combined host was routed by dragonfire at the Field of Fire. Rather than continue the fight, Loren submitted to Aegon the Conqueror, who confirmed him in his lands as Lord of Casterly Rock and Warden of the West. House Lannister has ruled the region from Casterly Rock ever since.
crownlands: The seat of the Iron Throne and the only region of the Seven Kingdoms ruled directly by the crown rather than through a great house sworn to it, centered on the city of King's Landing at the mouth of the Blackwater Rush. Before Aegon's Conquest the area had never formed a kingdom of its own, its scattered lands disputed between the Storm Kings of House Durrandon and the ironborn Kings of the Isles and the Rivers of House Hoare. Aegon Targaryen came ashore here with his sister-wives Rhaenys and Visenya, raised the wooden Aegonfort on the highest of three hills at his landing site, and chose to rule from the settlement growing around it rather than from Dragonstone or Oldtown, giving King's Landing its name and making it the capital of the new realm. The swords of the lords who submitted to him were melted down and forged into the Iron Throne. The Crownlands and its capital have since remained at the center of the Seven Kingdoms' history, most notably as the site of extensive fighting during the Dance of the Dragons, and as the target of the final campaign of Robert's Rebellion, which ended with the fall of King's Landing and the end of Targaryen rule there.
the-reach: The most populous and fertile of the Seven Kingdoms, held by House Tyrell from the castle of Highgarden. For thousands of years before Aegon's Conquest it was ruled by the Gardener Kings, one of the oldest and most powerful royal lines of Westeros. The dynasty ended when King Mern IX Gardener and nearly all his kin died at the Field of Fire, burned alongside the army of the Reach by Aegon's dragons. Harlen Tyrell, hereditary steward of Highgarden, surrendered the castle to Aegon the Conqueror rather than continue the fight, and was rewarded with the castle and dominion over the Reach as Lord Paramount of the Mander. House Tyrell remained a comparatively minor lordly house for generations until Robert's Rebellion, when Lord Mace Tyrell led the Reach's armies in a long but ultimately unsuccessful siege of Storm's End. After the rebellion's end, he and his bannermen swore fealty to the victorious King Robert Baratheon, and House Tyrell's standing at court rose considerably in the years that followed.
country-lhazar: A region of semi-arid pasture and hill country south of the Dothraki Sea and north of Slaver's Bay, home to the Lhazareen, a settled people of shepherds and farmers. Unlike their Dothraki neighbors, the Lhazareen renounce violence entirely and go about unarmed, worshipping the Great Shepherd, a god who teaches that all people are one flock; his temples are tended by priestess-healers known as godswives, who by their faith's tenets treat the sick and wounded regardless of who they are. The Dothraki hold the Lhazareen in open contempt, calling them haesh rakhi, "the lamb men," and consider raiding their undefended towns and enslaving their people fair game, since the Lhazareen refuse to take up arms even in their own defense. Captives taken in these raids are frequently sold on to the slave traders of the Ghiscari cities to the south, making Lhazar one of the principal wellsprings of Slaver's Bay's slave markets. Despite centuries of such raids, the Lhazareen have never taken up arms in retaliation, holding to their faith's demand of nonviolence even at great and repeated cost to themselves.
country-the-summer-isles: An archipelago in the Summer Sea south of Westeros, made up of three large islands — Walano, Jhala, and Omboru — along with many smaller ones, home to a graceful, dark-skinned people famed as sailors, archers, and lovers. Each of the three main islands is large enough to support several rival princedoms rather than a single crown, and losing princes are traditionally expected to accept exile rather than continue a defeated war. Walano's Tall Trees Town serves as the islands' cultural and religious heart, where priestesses carve the Summer Islanders' histories and laws into a grove of sacred Talking Trees, while Jhala, the largest of the three, stretches some two hundred leagues from end to end, its interior a tangle of emerald mountains and jungle valleys. The islands export exotic spices, fine hardwoods, sweet amber and palm wine, and the bright plumage that Summer Islanders themselves wear as long feathered cloaks, along with monkeys, apes, and other animals once prized by Valyrian dragonlords for their menageries. For nearly two centuries, known bitterly as the Years of Shame, the islands were preyed upon by slavers from Valyria, Old Ghis, and the Basilisk Isles, with some island princes even selling defeated rivals into bondage. That era ended when Princess Xanda Qo, once a slave herself, united the islands, armed her sailors with sturdy goldenheart-wood bows to match the slavers' own, and designed the first swan ships; her daughter, Chatana Qo, then led the Summer Islanders through a generation of war that finally broke the slavers' hold on the islands.
country-kingdom-of-sarnor: A once-mighty kingdom of city-states in the grasslands of north-central Essos, built along the great river Sarne and the lakes remaining from the vanished Silver Sea, ruled from its capital, Sarnath, by a line of High Kings. The Sarnori — who called themselves the Tall Men, or Tagaez Fen in their own tongue — traced their descent from the legendary king Huzhor Amai, said to be born of the last of the Fisher Queens; long-limbed and dark-eyed, they rode coal-black mares, and their finest warriors went to war in scythed chariots, often driven by their own wives or daughters, for among the Tall Men husbands and wives made war together. At its height Sarnor ruled all the lands watered by the Sarne and the Silver Sea's remnants, and fifty leagues beyond — said to have been the largest kingdom the world had yet seen. Rather than resist the Dothraki as they rose to power, the Tall Men tried to use Khal Mengo's horde as a weapon in their own wars; Mengo, acting on his mother Doshi's counsel, took whatever cities were offered to him and kept the conquered lands for himself besides. Over the following century, Dothraki khalasars destroyed Sarnor's cities one by one — Sathar fell first, Kasath six years later, then Gornath; the defenders of Mardosh held out for six years before starvation forced them to slay their own wives and children rather than see them enslaved, and rode out to die in one last charge. When the surviving Sarnori finally united against the invaders, four khalasars numbering eighty thousand riders crushed them in the battle remembered as the Field of Crows, between Sarnath and the ruins of Kasath, and a fortnight later Sarnath itself was stormed and put to the torch. Only the city of Saath survived the century-long slaughter; there, fewer than twenty thousand descendants of the Tall Men still call themselves Tagaez Fen and worship the gods of a kingdom that once numbered in the millions.
country-omber: A small, peaceable kingdom on a peninsula of northern Essos jutting into the Shivering Sea, bordered by the Bay of Tusks to the east, lying northeast of the Kingdom of Sarnor and west of the Kingdoms of the Ifeqevron. Its timid rulers and weak princes are known chiefly for the tribute — grain, gems, and slave girls — that they pay the Dothraki each year to spare their lands from ruin. Despite the similar name, Omber has no connection to House Umber of Last Hearth in the North of Westeros; the two are unrelated.
country-ibben: An archipelago nation in the far northwest of Essos, in the Shivering Sea, dominated by the large island of Ib along with several smaller islands. Ibben has no king; it is governed collectively by a small number of immensely wealthy trading families, whose combined assembly elects the ruling council seated at the Port of Ibben. Its economy rests almost entirely on whaling, with Ibbenese ships ranging across the Shivering Sea and into the icy waters beyond in pursuit of their catch, and on the whale oil, bone, and ivory traded from it to the rest of the known world. The Ibbenese themselves are a short, stocky, heavily built people, often remarked on by outsiders for their unusually thick body hair, and are widely regarded as reclusive, keeping close to their own islands and limiting contact with foreign visitors. Some maesters consider Ibben one of the oldest continuously settled realms known, though its early history remains poorly documented outside its own islands.
country-kingdoms-of-the-ifeqevron: A stretch of dense forest along the northern coast of Essos, in the far northeast near Ib and the Grey Waste, once home to the scattered petty kingdoms of the Ifeqevron. This small, shy, forest-dwelling people are believed by many maesters to be distantly kin to the children of the forest of Westeros, though little is recorded of their society beyond their retreat from the outside world. The Ifeqevron's Dothraki name — meaning roughly "those who wander among the trees" — outlived the people themselves; today the region is remembered chiefly through the ruins scattered across it, including their last known dwelling and an Ibbenese colony later built and destroyed in the same woods. Whether the Ifeqevron were driven out by Ibbenese settlers, exterminated in some forgotten conflict, or simply vanished into the depths of the forest is not known.
country-ghiscar: The desert peninsula of southeastern Essos framed by Slaver's Bay, homeland of the Ghiscari people and the site of the ancient Old Empire of Ghis before its destruction by Valyrian dragonfire. Today the region is dominated by the three Slaver Cities of Astapor, Yunkai, and Meereen, raised in the old empire's image amid the ruins of Old Ghis itself and a scatter of lesser settlements. Its economy has for centuries turned on the slave trade, supplying bed slaves, fighting slaves, and the eunuch soldiers known as the Unsullied to buyers across the known world. Ghiscar's arid, sun-scorched plains lie exposed to the Dothraki Sea to the north, leaving its cities and caravans perennially at risk from passing khalasars. Though the old Ghiscari tongue survives only in scattered words and in the ancient glyphs still used for writing, most Ghiscari today speak a corrupted form of High Valyrian, a legacy of the region's long subjugation, first by the Valyrian Freehold and later by Volantis during the Century of Blood.
country-yi-ti: A vast and ancient civilization occupying much of eastern Essos along the shores of the Jade Sea, generally reckoned one of the oldest and most sophisticated societies in the known world. Yi Ti is not a single city but a great many provinces and lesser lords bound together under the Golden Empire, whose throne has been held at various times by the cities of Yin, Jinqi, and Tiqui. Its nobility marks rank through an elaborate hierarchy of colors, echoed in the shifting hues of its ruling dynasties — grey, indigo, pearl-white, and now azure. Yi Ti is renowned across the known world for its silk, jade, and spices, and for scholarship far in advance of the west's: its astronomers are said to have charted eclipses and the courses of comets centuries before such things were understood in Westeros. Its southern neighbor, the island of Leng, was once a colony of Yi Ti before breaking away some four centuries ago, while the Five Forts guard its distant northeastern frontier against raiders out of the wastes beyond. To the west and south, Yi Ti's merchants ply the Jade Sea and the waters beyond in trade networks reaching as far as Qarth and Asshai, carrying home word — and coin — from across the known world.
country-realm-of-jhogwin: A region of far eastern Essos, named for the Jhogwin, an extinct race of giants said to have once ranged there, twice the size of the giants known in Westeros and reputed to have stood twenty to twenty-eight feet tall. Little remains of the Jhogwin today but their enormous bones, scattered across the region as the only evidence of their former presence. According to legend, the Jogos Nhai wiped out the last of the Jhogwin centuries ago in a decisive battle remembered as the Battle of the Howling Hills, led by a warlord recalled as Gharak Crookeye.
country-patrimony-of-hyrkoon: A once-fertile region of eastern Essos in the Bone Mountains beyond the Jade Sea, watered by rivers and lakes in ages past but now given over in its heart to the Great Sand Sea, a waste of barren dunes, dry riverbeds, and ruined towers where the southern reaches have grown so hot that all standing water has boiled away. To hold its western marches against outlaws, exiled men, and the wild mountain peoples of the Bone Mountains, the realm raised three fortress cities — Kayakayanaya, Samyriana, and Bayasabhad — each still ruled today by hereditary rulers known as the Great Fathers, whose daughters are trained from childhood as warriors while their sons are gelded on reaching manhood. The Patrimony is said to take its name from Hyrkoon the Hero, remembered as one of the many names given across the known world to the legendary Azor Ahai, though little else of his story has survived. Long past its height, the wider realm has since fallen into decline, its three fortress cities enduring as the last vestiges of a once-greater power.
country-n-ghai: The remnant of a once-proud ancient kingdom in the far northeast of Essos, bordered by the forests of Mossovy to the east, the plains of the Jogos Nhai to the west, the Cannibal Sands to the south, and the Thousand Islands to the north. Repeated wars and raids by the Jogos Nhai — a people who share close kinship with the inhabitants of N'Ghai despite the enmity between them — reduced the kingdom over the centuries from a wide realm to the single fortified city of Nefer and its immediate surroundings, the last redoubt of a once much larger civilization. Corlys Velaryon, later called the Sea Snake, was the first Westerosi known to have reached N'Ghai's shores, opening one of the earliest points of contact between Westeros and this remote corner of Essos.
country-jogos-nhai: A vast, arid grassland east of the Bones in far eastern Essos, home to the nomadic Jogos Nhai, a proud, restless, and warlike people who prize their freedom above all else. Rather than horses, they ride zorses — striped, hardy animals bred generations ago by crossing horses with zebras imported from Yi Ti, perfectly suited to their harsh homeland. Leadership is divided between two roles rather than resting with a single chief: a war leader called a jhat commands in times of conflict, while a moon singer — a shaman who serves as healer, judge, and spiritual guide — rules in peacetime; unusually, gender bends to the role rather than the reverse, as women may become jhats if they live and dress as men, and men may become moon singers if they take on a woman's dress and manner. Custom forbids the Jogos Nhai from shedding the blood of their own kin, so raids between rival bands are largely ritual affairs aimed at stealing livestock and spouses rather than taking lives. The Jogos Nhai have waged near-constant war against their neighbors, most bitterly against the Golden Empire of Yi Ti and against the kingdom of N'Ghai, which their raids brought to the edge of ruin.
country-mossovy: A cold, densely forested land in the far northeast of Essos, near the Grey Waste, considered by many in Westeros and the Free Cities to mark the very edge of the known world; some septons claim the world itself ends beyond its forests. Mossovy has a grim reputation as a gloomy realm of werewolves and demon hunters, though what manner of creatures actually haunt its woods, if any, remains unknown even to those who study such things. It has its own king, of whom little else is recorded. In 49 AC, Princess Alysanne Targaryen jested that even if her husband exiled her to marry the King of Mossovy or some lord of the Grey Waste, her dragon Silverwing would always carry her back to him — a remark that captures just how remote and undesirable the realm was held to be.
country-leng: An island region in the Jade Sea south of Yi Ti, home to the Lengii, said to be the tallest people in the known world, some standing seven or eight feet tall, with slender frames, teak-colored skin, and large golden eyes rumored to grant them superior night vision. Leng broke free of Yi Ti's Golden Empire some four centuries ago and has since been ruled by a line of divine empresses; by tradition, each empress takes two husbands, one drawn from the Yi Tish settlers of the island's north and one from the native Lengii of the south, a practice meant to honor both peoples equally. The current dynasty traces itself to Kiara the Great, still revered across the east as its founder. Leng's chief settlements include Leng Yi on the northern coast, Leng Ma on the central western shore, and the southern port of Turrani. The island's jungles are said to hold "ten thousand tigers and ten million monkeys," in the words of the travel-writer Lomas Longstrider. According to the Jade Compendium, ancient beings dwelling beneath Leng's subterranean ruins have on several occasions commanded the reigning empress to have foreign merchants put to death, feeding the island's forbidding reputation among outsiders. The Lengii speak their own dialect of the Yi Tish tongue and have long shown little interest in foreign trade or customs, historically keeping outsiders from exploiting the island's resources.
country-valyrian-freehold: A civilization of dragonlords that dominated most of Essos for five thousand years, technically a Freehold governed by its freeborn landowners rather than a king or emperor, though in practice power rested with some forty great dragonlord families who bred and rode dragons and who, gathering in Valyria, at times elected archons from among their own number to lead for limited terms. The Valyrians began as sheepherders on the Valyrian peninsula until they discovered dragons lairing in the Fourteen Fires and tamed them through sorcery, turning the beasts into instruments of conquest. Using slave labor to mine gold and silver from beneath the volcanoes and to build roads and cities, the Freehold expanded west and south, defeating the Old Empire of Ghis across five Ghiscari wars and crushing the Rhoynar in the Rhoynish Wars. Most of the modern Free Cities began as its colonies — Volantis, the eldest, founded as a military outpost and styled the "First Daughter" of Valyria, the others founded by merchants, pleasure-seekers, or religious refugees — with only Braavos founded in defiance of the Freehold, by slaves fleeing its rule. Valyrian dragonlords fused stone with dragonfire to build the great roads linking their cities, and Valyrian smiths forged blades of Valyrian steel, a secret since lost. Roughly a century before Aegon's Conquest, the Doom of Valyria annihilated the capital and killed nearly every dragonlord in a single catastrophic day, ending the Freehold's dominion outright. The chaos that followed, remembered as the Century of Blood, saw its former colonies fight over the vacuum it left behind, while House Targaryen, a minor dragonlord family that had already withdrawn to Dragonstone, alone survived to carry Valyrian blood and dragons into Westeros.
region-barrowlands: A region of wide, hilly plains in the North blanketed by hundreds of ancient barrows, the burial mounds of the First Men, with the town of Barrowton — seat of House Dustin — built around one of them, north of the Saltspear. That mound, the Great Barrow, is said by some to hold the grave of the First King, the first of the First Men to lead his people into Westeros, though others credit it instead to a King of the Giants. House Dustin claims descent from the ancient Barrow Kings who once ruled the region, a line said to trace back to that same First King. Singers tell of a Thousand Years War fought between the Barrow Kings and the Kings of Winter, though the conflict was likely a series of shorter wars spanning some two centuries rather than a single millennium. When the last Barrow King finally submitted to Winterfell, the victorious Stark king took his daughter to wife, and House Dustin — already carrying Barrow King blood — was raised to rule the Barrowlands from Barrow Hall in the Starks' name, a position it has held ever since.
region-the-rills: A hilly region on the North's western coast, lying between the Barrowlands to the east and the Stony Shore to the northwest, its name reflecting the many small streams and brooks that thread through it. It is held today by House Ryswell, vassals of House Stark, though for generations before them the Rills were ruled by House Ryder as First Men petty kings who rose after the Long Night, until they bent the knee to the Kings of Winter and became their vassals instead. During the reign of King Theon Stark, the Rills rose in a brief rebellion that Stark put down before it could spread. In a later generation, Lord Rodrik Ryswell and his children carried the family's famous quarrelsomeness so far that, as the local joke went, they could not even agree on which of their own house colors to wear.
region-the-land-of-always-winter: The northernmost known reach of Westeros, lying beyond the Frostfangs and the great lakes that separate it from the haunted forest, near the valley of Thenn. Permanently locked in ice and largely unmapped, it has never been explored by the peoples of the Seven Kingdoms. According to legend, it was from this frozen waste that the Others emerged during the Long Night, and it is still widely believed to be their point of origin.
region-the-neck: The narrow, marshy isthmus joining the North to the rest of Westeros, a natural land bridge between the Sunset Sea and the Narrow Sea covered almost entirely in bog, reed-choked swamp, and quicksand. It is ruled by House Reed on behalf of the crannogmen, a small, reclusive First Men people who live in villages of woven reed and thatch built atop floating islands called crannogs, subsisting on fish, frogs, and the lizard-lions they hunt from narrow boats. The Reeds' own seat, Greywater Watch, is said to be no ordinary castle at all but a moving stronghold that drifts among the Neck's rivers and lakes, impossible for ravens or strangers to find unguided. The crannogmen's unusually short stature is popularly attributed to old intermarriage with the children of the forest, with whom they grew especially close in the days when the greenseers tried to bring the Hammer of the Waters down upon the Neck itself. For thousands of years the crannogmen answered only to their own Marsh Kings, until King Rickard Stark slew the last of that line in single combat and took his daughter to wife, after which the crannogmen bent the knee to Winterfell and House Reed rose to lead them as loyal Stark bannermen. The Neck's bogs and hidden causeways — winding trails between quagmires known only to the crannogmen, and wet roads through the reeds passable solely by boat — have made it one of the most effective natural defenses in Westeros. At its narrowest point stand the ruins of Moat Cailin, whose walls, working together with the surrounding swamp, broke every army that tried to force its way north; during the Andal invasion, the crannogmen and Moat Cailin's defenders threw back every assault, and the fortress never fell to the invaders by storm.
region-the-flatlands: A fertile stretch of open fields and plains in western Essos, controlled by the Free City of Pentos and largely responsible for feeding it. Bounded by the Velvet Hills to the north, the Golden Fields to the southeast, and the upper Rhoyne to the east, the region is worked by tillers and toilers bound to the land, while many of Pentos's magisters and nobles keep country estates here. Before the Andals' migration to Westeros, the Flatlands formed part of the southern marches of Andalos, their ancestral kingdom; most of that territory later passed under Pentoshi control. An old Valyrian road runs through the region, linking Pentos to the ruined city of Ghoyan Drohe. Lying open to Dothraki riders, the Flatlands have long obliged Pentos's magisters, like those of the other Free Cities, to pay the horselords heavy tribute to keep their estates and villages from being raided.
region-the-disputed-lands: A fertile but perpetually contested region of southwestern Essos, claimed in turn by the neighboring Free Cities of Lys, Myr, and Tyrosh, none of which has ever managed to hold it for long. Once rich farmland under the Valyrian Freehold, it was ravaged into a wasteland during the Century of Blood that followed the Doom, when the three cities tore at each other and at Volantis for control of it. Rather than risk their own citizens, the Lyseni, Myrish, and Tyroshi have for centuries hired sellswords to fight their border wars for them, a practice that has made the Disputed Lands the birthplace of more free companies than anywhere else in the known world — some two score are said to campaign there at any given time. Among the most celebrated of these is the Golden Company, founded by the exiled Aegor Rivers and quickly recognized as the foremost free company in the region, though it has since carried its banners as far as Westeros itself. The endless, indecisive wars fought here have made the Disputed Lands a byword for mercenary warfare: a place where loyalty is bought and sold, and where the true winners are rarely the three cities themselves but the companies they hire.
region-lands-of-the-long-summer: A region of southern central Essos, bordering the Sea of Sighs near Mantarys and reaching south to the shore of the Smoking Sea. Once an integral part of the Valyrian Freehold, it was left an isolated backwater when the Doom of Valyria tore the peninsula apart, separating these lands from Valyria itself across the new-formed Smoking Sea. A Valyrian road still runs through the region, linking Mantarys in the north to the ruined city of Oros on the Smoking Sea's northern coast — a city once said to rival Valyria itself in splendor before the Doom, whose ruins remain inhabited today by descendants of uncertain lineage, of whom travelers tell only unsettling tales.
region-three-sisters: A cluster of three islands — Sweetsister, Longsister, and Littlesister — lying in the Bite off the northern coast of the Vale of Arryn. They are ruled by House Sunderland, sworn to House Arryn as Warden of the East, with the lesser houses Borrell of Sweetsister, Longthorpe of Longsister, and Torrent of Littlesister sworn beneath them in turn. The Sistermen have long been known for a dialect and customs distinct from the rest of the Vale, and for a reputation — not entirely undeserved — as wreckers and smugglers; Sisterton itself is considered one of the most notorious smuggling havens in the Seven Kingdoms. For nearly a thousand years the islands were fought over by the Vale's Kings of Mountain and Vale and the Kings in the North, in a long, sporadic conflict remembered as the War Across the Water, or derisively as the Meaningless War, whose grimmest chapter was a northern fleet's harsh reconquest of the isles known as the Ravaging of the Three Sisters. The Sistermen eventually swore fealty to House Arryn in exchange for aid against a northern invasion, but that fealty proved shallow: at the outset of Aegon's Conquest, the lords of the Three Sisters renounced young King Ronnel Arryn and proclaimed Lady Marla Sunderland their queen in the short-lived Sistermen's Rebellion. Aegon the Conqueror had Torrhen Stark, newly made Warden of the North, put down the revolt; a northern host under Ser Warrick Manderly sailed for the Sisters, and the sudden appearance of Queen Visenya Targaryen on her dragon Vhagar broke what resistance remained, leading the Sistermen to depose Marla themselves and restore their fealty to the Eyrie under her brother Steffon.
region-shield-islands: A chain of four small islands in the Sunset Sea off the western coast of the Reach, positioned to guard the mouth of the Mander from raiders sailing in from the sea. Each island is held by its own vassal house sworn to Highgarden: Oakenshield, the easternmost of the four and closest to the Mander's mouth, is the seat of House Hewett at Lord Hewett's Town; Greenshield, the northernmost, is held by House Chester; Southshield, in the south, by House Serry; and Greyshield by House Grimm. Together the four houses form the Reach's first line of defense against seaborne raiders, their small castles and levies meant to blunt or delay an incursion long enough for Highgarden's greater strength to respond. Despite this purpose, the islands' modest garrisons have not always been able to withstand a determined seaborne assault, leaving them among the more exposed points along the Reach's coastline.
region-the-princes-pass: One of the two principal mountain routes through the Red Mountains linking Dorne to the Reach and stormlands beyond, less steep and treacherous than its southern counterpart, the Boneway. Its Dornish end is watched over by the castle of Skyreach, seat of House Fowler, who hold the hereditary title Warden of the Prince's Pass. During the First Dornish War, Aegon the Conqueror divided his host at the pass's far end, sending one column south toward the Hellholt while leading the other east to Skyreach itself, even as Queen Rhaenys Targaryen flew her dragon Meraxes over the mountains to raid Vaith and Godsgrace beyond. Centuries later, during King Daeron I's conquest of Dorne, Lord Lyonel Tyrell led one of three invading hosts through the Prince's Pass, entering Dorne at the western end of the Red Mountains.
region-the-shadow-lands: A remote and forbidding region at the far eastern edge of Essos, beyond the Mountains of the Morn, through which the Ash River flows down to the port of Asshai on the Jade Sea. Little of the Shadow Lands beyond Asshai-by-the-Shadow has ever been explored, since few travelers venture far upriver and fewer still return to tell of it. Deeper within lies Stygai, a ruined city said to be older and more terrible than Asshai itself, and the region is widely held to be haunted by demons and darker things still, its very earth touched by ancient, malevolent sorcery. Even Asshai's own shadowbinders, practitioners of the blackest magic known to the world, are said to fear venturing far into the Shadow proper, leaving most of the region entirely unmapped and unknown beyond rumor and dread.
region-cities-of-the-bloodless-men: A little-known region of far eastern Essos, lying between the Dry Deep and the Mountains of the Morn, home to a cluster of cities inhabited by the Bloodless Men. Little is certain about this people beyond their name, which travelers explain in one of two ways: that it refers to the extraordinary paleness of their skin, or that the Bloodless Men are literally drained corpses restored to a kind of life through dark sorcery. Their cities remain unnamed and undescribed in the accounts that survive, and no further history of the region is recorded.
region-land-of-the-shrykes: A plain in the Grey Waste of far eastern Essos, lying beyond the Five Forts on the eastern shore of the Bleeding Sea, home to the reclusive Shrykes. Little else about the Shrykes or their land has been recorded, and even their nature is disputed: some accounts describe them as humanoid half-men, half-lizards with green scaled skin whose bite is venomous, while others hold that they are simply men who wear the skins of lizards. The region is widely regarded as a dangerous place that travelers give a wide berth.
region-dornish-marches: The borderlands of southwestern Stormlands and southeastern Reach that abut Dorne, a country of windswept downs, grasslands, and the occasional swamp, with fewer of the storms that lash the coast further east. The Eastern March, guarding the Stormlands' Dornish border, is held by four principal houses — the Carons of Nightsong, who still claim the old title Lord of the Marches; the Swanns of Stonehelm; the Dondarrions of Blackhaven; and the Selmys of Harvest Hall — while other houses along the Reach's own stretch of the border share the same marcher heritage. Marcher lords are said to be born with a sword in hand, and their castles rank among the strongest in Westeros, built to withstand generations of raiding across the mountains. Long before Aegon's Conquest unified the Seven Kingdoms, the Marches stood as the front line shielding the Stormlands and the Reach from Dornish incursions, while marcher lords rode the other way in kind, and the region's warriors won a lasting reputation for ferocity and skill at arms, hunting down bandits and outlaws who took refuge in the Red Mountains. Since the Conquest bound Dorne to the rest of the realm, the Marches have lost much of their old military importance, though marcher folk have kept their combative reputation.
region-thenn: A hidden valley deep in the Frostfangs beyond the Wall, home to the Thenns, a First Men people set apart from the rest of the free folk by their rigid, hereditary rule and unusual craft. Where most wildling clans follow a chief only so long as he proves himself, the Thenns submit to their Magnar — an ancient First Men title meaning lord or chieftain — with an iron discipline bordering on worship, obeying him almost as they would a god. Alone among the peoples beyond the Wall, the Thenns still work copper and tin into bronze, arming themselves with metal weapons, armor, and horns where other clans make do with wood, stone, and scavenged steel, and their fierce discipline has made them widely feared as the most dangerous warriors north of the Wall. They are also among the last to speak the Old Tongue of the First Men fluently, most other wildlings knowing only scraps of the Common Speech, and are said to keep closer company with the giants of the far north than do other free folk. Their isolation in Thenn's high valley has preserved customs and skills long lost elsewhere beyond the Wall, making them as much a curiosity as a threat to those who venture near.
region-andalos: The ancestral homeland of the Andals, a region of northwestern Essos bounded by the Narrow Sea to the west, Braavos to the north, and the Hills of Norvos to the east. Its western reaches are flat plains, growing hillier further east around the Velvet Hills, and the headwaters of the Upper Rhoyne and the Lesser Rhoyne both rise here. The Andals, who may have originated on the Axe, drove out an earlier people known as the hairy men and built a kingdom here under Hugor of the Hill, whom the Seven are said to have crowned in Andalos's hills. Tradition holds that the Faith of the Seven and the trial of seven both originated in this land, and that the Seven's promise of kingdoms in a foreign country later drove the Andals to cross the Narrow Sea into Westeros, where they overthrew many of the First Men's kingdoms. Pressed westward by Valyria's expansion, most Andals eventually abandoned Andalos altogether, and much of its territory has since passed under the control of the Free City of Pentos.
